rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root originally means confronting someone with a false accusation; bewilderment under decisive proof is figuratively called bahat because it resembles the accused person's confusion. ʿUrwa's verse uses it for being stunned and falling silent.
rows.anchor: فما هو إلا أن أراها فجاءة ... فأبهت حتى ما أكاد أجيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb has three forms: bahita with passive participle mabhuut, and the alternatives bahata and bahuta.
rows.anchor: وفيه ثلاث لغات: بهت الرجل فهو مبهوت، وبهت، وبهت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here the disbeliever was defeated by the argument, stopped speaking, and fell silent.
rows.anchor: وتأويل قوله (¬4): فبهت أي: انقطع وسكت

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq gives one parse of rasūlan as coordinated with a verb meaning “make him a messenger.”
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق (¬2): ينتصب على وجهين: أحدهما: (ويجعله (¬3) رسولا)

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq prefers parsing rasūlan with “speaks to the people,” since the following words mean “I have come to you”; Jesus addresses them as a messenger.
rows.anchor: قال أبو إسحاق (¬2): ينتصب على وجهين: أحدهما: (ويجعله (¬3) رسولا). قال: والاختيار عندي: أنه (ويكلم الناس رسولا)

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash allows an inserted conjunction and takes rasūlan as a circumstantial accusative describing the pronoun in “we teach him the Book.”
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش (¬6): إن شئت جعلت الواو في {ورسولا} مقحمة (¬7)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the wording says one sign, Jesus brought several: forming a bird, curing the blind-born and leper, raising the dead, and telling what people ate. The author takes bird-making as the sign, then treats the cures and other miracles as a new sentence.
rows.anchor: وهي: خلق الطير، وإبراء الأكمه والأبرص، وإحياء الموتى، وإنباء (¬2) بما يأكلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥ on annī, the clause is an appositive to āya, understood as “I came to you with my creating”; it may be genitive as an appositive or nominative with the sense “the sign is that I create.”
rows.anchor: كأنه قال: (وجئتكم بأني أخلق لكم من الطين)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With kasr on innī, one parse starts a new sentence and breaks it from what precedes.
rows.anchor: ومن كسر (¬9)، فله وجهان: أحدهما: الاستئناف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other kasr parse makes “I create for you” explain the sign; the author prefers it because it matches the fatḥ reading in meaning, as in the cited explanatory clauses.
rows.anchor: وهذا الوجه أحسن؛ لأنه في المعنى كقراءة من فتح (أني)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here create means to determine and shape; in Arabic, creation can mean estimation.
rows.anchor: أخلق لكم من الطين} أي: أقدر، وأصور. والخلق، معناه: التقدير في اللغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hayʾa means a formed image, from the verb “to shape or determine a thing.”
rows.anchor: الهيئة: الصورة المهيأة؛ من قولهم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭayr may be masculine when treated as a collective noun or feminine when treated as a group noun.
rows.anchor: و (الطير): يجوز تذكيره، على معنى الجمع، وتأنيثه، على معنى الجماعة.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun cannot refer to the general word clay: the breath goes into a particular piece shaped from clay, not all the clay previously mentioned.
rows.anchor: ولا يجوز أن تعود (¬2) الكناية (¬3) إلى الطين؛ لأن النفخ إنما يكون في طين مخصوص

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: One possible antecedent is the shaped object: “the form” stands for the thing possessing that form, as “the portion” can mean what is apportioned in 4:8.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تعود الكناية على ذي الهيئة. وأريد ب (الهيئة): ذو الهيئة، كما أريد ب (القسمة): المقسوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Ali's option lets the pronoun refer to the creation implied by “I create,” with creation standing for the created thing.
rows.anchor: فيكون قوله: {فأنفخ فيه}؛ أي: في الخلق، ويكون الخلق بمنزلة المخلوق

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: It can instead refer to the likeness implied by the kāf: the meaning is “I create a creation like the form of a bird,” with the kāf describing an implied verbal noun.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تعود إلى ما دل عليه الكاف من معنى المثل؛ لأن المعنى: أخلق من الطين مثل هيئة الطير

rows.speaker: نافع
rows.claim: Nafi reads ṭāʾiran; it can mean that what Jesus blows into or forms becomes a bird, or that each thing formed becomes a bird, as in the expression “eighty lashes” for each person receiving eighty.
rows.anchor: وقرأ (¬7) نافع (¬8): {طائرا} (¬9)

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say Nafi chose the singular because Jesus created only one kind of bird, the bat, which they regarded as the most fully formed bird.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم (¬4): ذهب نافع (¬5) إلى نوع واحد من الطير؛ لأنه لم يخلق غير الخفاش

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb reports that the bird flew while people watched, then fell dead when it went out of their sight.
rows.anchor: قال وهب: كان يطير ما دام الناس ينظرون

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: Al-Aṣmaʿī assigns bariʾtu to Tamim speech and baraʾtu to the people of the Hijaz.
rows.anchor: قال الأصمعي (¬2): برئت من المرض: لغة تميم، وبرأت: لغة أهل الحجاز

rows.speaker: أبو زيد
rows.claim: Abu Zayd reverses the regional attribution for baraʾtu and says the rest of the Arabs use bariʾtu.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو زيد (¬4): برأت من المرض: لغة أهل الحجاز

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Qatada define al-akmah as someone born blind who never saw light.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، وقتادة (¬2): هو الذي ولد أعمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-abraṣ is a person afflicted with a white skin patch or discoloration.
rows.anchor: والأبرص: الذي به وضح

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi recounts that Jesus revived Lazarus, his friend; called Sam son of Noah from his grave; and prayed for a dead young man on a bier, who rose, returned to his family, lived, and had children.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي (¬6): كان (¬7) عيسى عليه السلام يحيي الأموات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “what you eat and store,” mā means “that which”: what you eat and what you store.
rows.anchor: (ما) بمعنى: الذي؛ أي: بالذي تأكلونه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A tafsir gloss says Jesus told them what they ate in the morning and what they kept for the rest of the day.
rows.anchor: وجاء (¬3) في التفسير: بما تأكلون في غدوكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taddakhirūn is on the iftaʿala pattern from dhukhr, “storing”: the original iztakhara changes tāʾ to voiced dāl after voiced dhāl, then assimilates dhāl into dāl. The author gives similar consonant adjustments in izdajara, iḍṭarra, and iṣṭabara.
rows.anchor: وأصله: (اذتخر) (¬6)، فأبدل (¬7) التاء دالا (¬8)

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil defines a voiced consonant as one articulated with firm contact that blocks breath, and a voiceless consonant as one with weaker contact through which breath flows.
rows.anchor: قال الخليل (¬1): الحرف (¬2) المجهور: الذي أشبع (¬3) الاعتماد (¬4) عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feared failure of justice among four wives concerns affection and sexual relations.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {فإن خفتم ألا تعدلوا}، أي: في الأربع، بالحب والجماع (¬5).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command means that each man should marry one woman.
rows.anchor: أي: فلينكح كل واحد منكم واحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the nominative reading, “one” means one woman is sufficient or satisfactory.
rows.anchor: ومن قرأ بالرفع (¬2) أراد: فواحدة مقنع، أو فواحدة رضا (¬3).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means female slaves, for they do not carry the same rights as free wives and are not owed an equal day-and-night rotation.
rows.anchor: وقوله تعالى: {أو ما ملكت أيمانكم}. يريد من الجواري (¬4)؛ لأنه لا يلزم فيهن من الحقوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “right hands” is explanatory here, with the sense simply “or what you own.”
rows.anchor: ومعنى الأيمان ههنا بيان، تقديره: أو ما ملكتم (¬6).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The demonstrative points back to “marry what is good to you”; limiting the number of wives is closer to justice and farther from oppression.
rows.anchor: الإشارة في {ذلك} تعود إلى قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author favors the established gloss “incline and act unjustly,” supported by the majority of exegetes and linguists, over the sense “have many dependents.”
rows.anchor: عن جميع أهل التفسير واللغة (¬3)

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha transmits the Prophet's gloss “do not oppress”; a second transmitted wording is “do not incline.”
rows.anchor: روت عائشة، عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - في قوله: {ذلك أدنى ألا تعولوا} قال: "لا تجوروا".

rows.speaker: ابن المظفر
rows.claim: Ibn al-Muẓaffar defines ʿawl as inclination in judgment toward injustice.
rows.anchor: قال ابن المظفر: العول الميل في الحكم إلى الجور (¬6).

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda, quoting al-Aṣmaʿī, says a balance that inclines is called ʿāla, deriving the word from injustice.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة، عن الأصمعي: وعال الميزان إذا مال، وإنما هو مأخوذ من الجور (¬7)

rows.speaker: أبو طالب
rows.claim: Abu Talib's verse uses ʿayl for a balance that does not lean and ʿāʾil for a measurer who is not unjust, illustrating the gloss of injustice.
rows.anchor: وأنشد لأبي طالب (¬8): بميزان قسط لا يعل شعيرة ... ووزان صدق وزنه غير عائل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وإبراهيم وقتادة والربيع والسدي وأبو مالك وعكرمة والفراء والزجاج وابن قتيبة وابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ glosses ʿāla yaʿūlu as to incline and act unjustly; Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Ibrahim, Qatada, al-Rabiʿ, al-Suddi, Abu Malik, ʿIkrima, al-Zajjaj, Ibn Qutayba, and Ibn al-Anbari share this view.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا القول ابن عباس، والحسن، وإبراهيم، وقتادة

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi says the phrase means “so that your dependents do not become numerous”; ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam also adopts this interpretation.
rows.anchor: عن الشافعي - رضي الله عنه - (¬3) أنه قال: معناه ألا يكثر عيالكم (¬4)

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi says some eloquent Arabs use ʿāla yaʿūlu for having many dependents, which shows that al-Shafiʿi's reading has a linguistic basis.
rows.anchor: عن الفراء، عن الكسائي (¬8)، أنه قال: ومن العرب الفصحاء من يقول: عال يعول

rows.speaker: الكسائي والأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi confirms that ʿāla for having many dependents is eloquent Arabic he heard from Arabs; al-Azhari says this vindicates al-Shafiʿi linguistically.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي: وهي لغة فصيحة سمعتها من العرب (¬10). قال الأزهري (¬1): وهذا يدل على أن الشافعي لم يخطئ

rows.speaker: الأزهري
rows.claim: Al-Azhari distinguishes the familiar ʿāla yaʿūlu, “incline and act unjustly,” from aʿāla, “have many dependents.”
rows.anchor: قال الأزهري (¬1): وهذا يدل على أن الشافعي لم يخطئ من جهة اللغة؛ لأن الكسائي ثقة مأمون (¬2). قال (¬3): والمعروف من كلام العرب: عال الرجل يعول

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari finds a linguistic route for al-Shafiʿi's view by analogy with an inheritance share that increases: the dependents increase until one neglects their due obligations.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري: وهذا القول -على قلة القائلين به- له مخرج في اللغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the dependents gloss is linguistically possible, the author prefers “do not incline unjustly”: the permission for many slave women also brings expenses, and the answer must match the stated fear of failing justice, not poverty.
rows.anchor: وهذا القول وإن صح، فالاختيار القول الأول (¬10)، لقوله: {أو ما ملكت أيمانكم}

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses the phrase as “so that you do not go astray”; the author says this returns to the first interpretation because turning from the truth is error.
rows.anchor: وروي عن مجاهد أنه قال: معنى قوله: {ألا تعدلوا} ألا تضلوا (¬3). وهذا راجع إلى الأول

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj parses the command as God enjoining both worship of Him and kindness to parents.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج المعنى: أوصاكم الله بعبادته، وأوصاكم بالوالدين إحسانا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ expands the wording as an imperative: “and treat parents kindly.”
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: وأحسنوا بالوالدين إحسانا. أمرهم بالإحسان (¬5)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas describes filial kindness as gentle treatment: humble one's voice and gaze, answer softly, and stand before parents in loving humility like a servant before a harsh master, as in 17:24.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد البر بهما مع اللطف ولين الجانب، ولا يغلظ لهما الجواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurbā is a verbal noun like qarāba, as bushrā and rujʿā are verbal nouns.
rows.anchor: القربى مصدر كالقرابة (¬1)، ومثله البشرى والرجعى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says to maintain relations with and show affection to one's relatives.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يصله ويعطف عليه (¬2)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says God commands kindness to relatives after parents.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: أمر الله: عز وجل بالإحسان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says to treat orphans gently, draw them close, and stroke their heads.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يرفق بهم ويدنيهم ويمسح رأسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas recommends giving the poor what one can readily spare or returning them a kind response.
rows.anchor: يريد: بذل يسر، أو رد جميل (¬4)

rows.speaker: عامة المفسرين
rows.claim: Most exegetes identify the near neighbor as a neighbor related by blood, who is owed kinship, neighborly, and Islamic rights.
rows.anchor: قال عامة المفسرين: يعني القريب في النسب

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj takes nearness to mean a nearby home and familiarity; the nearby neighbor knows you, unlike the distant stranger mentioned next.
rows.anchor: ودل كلام الزجاج على أنه أراد بالقربى ههنا قرب الدار والمعرفة والاختلاط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the majority's kinship interpretation; he also notes that the contrast with the distant neighbor supports a proximity reading of al-jār dhī al-qurbā.
rows.anchor: والذي عليه المفسرون هو الأول.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Junub is an adjective on the fuʿl pattern, like aḥad in nāqa aḥad, ghalq, and fatḥ; it derives from janāba, the opposite of closeness, and means distance. ʿAlqama and al-Aʿshā use janāba in this sense.
rows.anchor: فلا تحرمني نائلا عن جنابة ... فإني امرؤ وسط القباب غريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root denotes removal and distancing; the author links it to Abraham's prayer that God keep him and his sons far from worshipping idols in 14:35.
rows.anchor: وأصل الجنب التنحية والإبعاد، ومنه قوله: {واجنبني وبني أن نعبد الأصنام} [إبراهيم: 35].

rows.speaker: المفضل عن عاصم
rows.claim: Al-Mufaḍḍal reports from ʿĀṣim a reading with fatḥ on jīm and sukūn on nūn; it can mean a neighbor from a distant side with the genitive noun omitted, or simply a distant stranger as an adjective.
rows.anchor: وروى المفضل عن عاصم (¬5): {والجار الجنب} بفتح الجيم وسكون النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the first reading, junub may mean “side,” with “possessor of a side” understood because a neighbor cannot itself be a side; alternatively it is an adjective like ḍarb, nadb, and fisal.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أن يريد بالجنب الناحية، ويكون المعنى على هذا: ذي الجنب، فحذف المضاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further cited line calls a stranger “a man junub” and pluralizes the adjective as ajnūb; junub is based on being removed and far away.
rows.anchor: ورجل جنب، إذا كان غريبا متباعدا عن أهله. وقوم أجناب، ورجل أجنب وأجنبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An anonymous poet describes noble people approached from afar as lenient to a neighboring guest, illustrating junāba as distance.
rows.anchor: وقال آخر: كرام إذا ما جئتهم عن جنابة ... أعفاء عن جار الخليط المجاور

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير ومجاهد وقتادة والحسن والسدي والضحاك
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and al-Dahhak identify the companion at one's side as a travel companion.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير ومجاهد وقتادة والحسن والسدي والضحاك: هو الرفيق في السفر (¬3)

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: ʿAtaʾ, quoting Ibn Abbas, says the travel companion beside you has both the right of neighborliness and the right of companionship.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس: يريد صاحبك في السفر، وهو جارك إلى جانبك، فله حق الجوار وحق الصحبة (¬4)

rows.speaker: الفراء والزجاج وابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ, al-Zajjaj, and Ibn Qutayba choose the travel-companion interpretation.
rows.anchor: وهذا اختيار الفراء (¬5) والزجاج (¬6) وابن قتيبة (¬7)

rows.speaker: علي وابن مسعود وابن أبي ليلى وإبراهيم
rows.claim: Ali, Ibn Masʿud, Ibn Abi Layla, and Ibrahim identify the companion at one's side as one's wife.
rows.anchor: وقال علي وابن مسعود وابن أبي ليلى (¬8) وإبراهيم: هو زوجتك تكون معك إلى جنبك (¬9)

rows.speaker: ابن جريج وابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd understand it as someone who stays close to you hoping for your help and benefit.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج وابن زيد: هو الذي يلزمك ويصحبك رجاء خيرك ونفعك (¬1)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The son of the road is a guest, whom one must host until he reaches his intended destination.
rows.anchor: {وابن السبيل}. هو الضيف، يجب قراه إلى أن يبلغ حيث يريد

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد والربيع
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Rabiʿ identify him as a passing traveler, whom one should give water and food until he leaves.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس ومجاهد والربيع: يريد عابر السبيل، ترويه وتطعمه حتى يرحل عنك (¬2)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase refers to enslaved people.
rows.anchor: {وما ملكت أيمانكم} يعني المماليك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says to feed an enslaved person well, bear mistakes, and forgive; if temperaments do not fit, sell him so he may suit another owner and you avoid wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد المملوك، تحسن رزقه وتحتمل مساوئه وتعفو عنه فيما يخطئ

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar reports the Prophet's instruction to sell a servant whose disposition does not suit the owner, keep looking until finding a match, and not torment God's servants because people have different temperaments.
rows.anchor: وروى عمر بن الخطاب أن رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - قال: "من ابتاع شيئا من الخدم فلم يوافق شيمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mukhtāl means a person possessed by conceit and arrogance.
rows.anchor: المختال: ذو الخيلاء والكبر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas describes the conceited person as self-important and failing to fulfill God's rights.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يريد بالمختال العظيم في نفسه، الذي لا يقوم بحقوق الله (¬1)

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj explains that conceit is mentioned because an arrogant person disdains poor relatives and neighbors and therefore treats them badly.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج: وإنما ذكر الاختيال ههنا، لأن المختال يأنف من ذوي قراباته إذا كانوا فقراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author refers readers to his earlier discussion of the derivation of khaylāʾ at 3:14.
rows.anchor: وذكرنا اشتقاقه في اللغة عند قوله: {والخيل المسومة} [آل عمران: 14].

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fakhr means boasting and overreaching; a fakhūr magnifies his merits out of arrogance.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الفخر في اللغة هو البذخ والتطاول، والفخور الذي يعدد مناقبه كبرا وتطاولا (¬3)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the boastful person flaunts before God's servants the honor and blessings God has granted him.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هو الذي يفخر على عباد الله بما خوله الله من كرامته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In yawmʾidhin, yawm is an adverb attached to idh; the tanwin compensates for an omitted genitive clause. Idh normally takes a following nominal or verbal clause, as in the cited examples.
rows.anchor: ودخل التنوين في إذ بدلا من الإضافة، وذلك أن أصل هذا أن تكون إذ مضافة إلى جملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kasra on the dhāl in idh is not case marking, even if idh is genitive; it breaks the two adjacent still consonants.
rows.anchor: فكسرت الذال لالتقاء الساكنين فقيل: يومئذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line ending “and you were then sound” shows idh used without anything preceding it, supporting the claim that its kasra is phonetic rather than case marking.
rows.anchor: نهيتك عن طلابك أم عمرو ... بعاقبة وأنت إذ صحيح

rows.speaker: القطامي
rows.claim: Al-Qutami's line illustrates idh attached to a clause beginning with a nominal predicate, as in the grammatical construction under discussion.
rows.anchor: وقال القطامي (¬4): إذا الفوارس من قيس بشكتها ... حولي شهود وما قومي بشهاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author refers to his earlier discussion of yawaddu at 2:96.
rows.anchor: ومضى القول في (يود) عند قوله:

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sikkit defines naqīr as the small mark on the back of a date stone.
rows.anchor: قال ابن السكيت: النقير النكتة في ظهر النواة (¬3)

rows.speaker: أبو الهيثم
rows.claim: Abu al-Haytham defines naqīr as the hollow on a date stone from which the palm grows.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الهيثم: النقير نقرة في ظهر النواة، منها تنبت النخلة (¬4)

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh calls sawfa a particle of respite, threat, and warning; he also notes the form saw without fāʾ.
rows.anchor: سيبويه: سوف أداة تنفيس وتهديد ووعيد

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another view derives sawfa from postponement: “I will give you” means later, not now; sīn can replace it. This reading takes the threat as future punishment and cites 74:26 and 93:5.
rows.anchor: وقال غيره: هي أداة التسويف، كأنها مأخوذة منه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some call sawfa a particle of causation, consequence, or confirmation; in 12:98, Joseph's promise is said to defer supplication until dawn to secure it.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم: سوف كلمة تعليل، وهي أيضا كلمة العقبى كهي في هذه الآية، وكلمة تحقيق أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author refers to earlier discussions of iṣlāʾ at 4:10 and “they will burn in a blazing fire.”
rows.anchor: وذكرنا ما في الإصلاء عند قوله: {وسيصلون سعيرا} [النساء: 10]

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says their replacement skins are white, like sheets of paper.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يبدلون جلودا بيضا كأمثال القراطيس (¬3)

rows.speaker: معاذ بن جبل
rows.claim: Muʿadh ibn Jabal says the skins are replaced one hundred times in an hour; the report is also transmitted as a Prophetic report through ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: وقال معاذ بن جبل (¬4): يبدل في ساعة مائة مرة. وروى ذلك مرفوعا عمر عن النبي

rows.speaker: جماعة من أهل المعاني
rows.claim: A group of language scholars, including al-Zajjaj, Ibn Kaysan, and Ibn al-Anbari, say that once the skins are cooked they are renewed to their unburned state; “other” can describe a changed form while the underlying substance remains the same.
rows.anchor: قال جماعة من أهل المعاني: إن جلودهم إذا نضجت واحترقت جددت، بأن ترد إلى الحال التي كانت عليها غير محترقة

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ illustrates two uses of baddala: replacing a ring with another object, and melting the ring into a hoop; in the latter, its material remains.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء: بدلت الخاتم بالحلقة إذا نحيت هذا وجعلت هذا مكانه

rows.speaker: أبو العباس أحمد بن يحيى
rows.claim: Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Yahya says tabdīl changes one form into another while preserving the same substance; ibdāl removes the original substance and substitutes a new one.
rows.anchor: قال أبو العباس: وحقيقته أن التبديل تغيير صورة إلى صورة أخرى، والجوهرة (¬4) بعينها

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad says Arabs sometimes use baddala for abdala, as in 25:70, where sins are removed and replaced by good deeds.
rows.anchor: قد جعلت العرب بدلت بمعنى أبدلت

words: كُلَّمَا نَضِجَتْ جُلُودُهُم بَدَّلْنَٰهُمْ جُلُودًا غَيْرَهَا
rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad applies the form-change sense here: the substance of the skin remains, but after blackening in torment its original form is restored; the author says this is supported by Ibn Abbas's report.
rows.anchor: وهذه هي الجوهرة بعينها باقية، وتبديلها تغيير صورتها إلى غيرها؛ لأنها كانت ناعمة فاسودت بالعذاب

rows.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
rows.claim: Abu Ali al-Farisi says baddala and abdala cannot be distinguished: in 16:101 the replaced verse may remain recited or be lifted, while in 34:16 both gardens remain.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو علي الفارسي: ليس ينفصل (بدل) من (أبدل) بشيء، فقد يقال: تبدل في الشيء

rows.speaker: جماعة
rows.claim: Some take the wording literally: God creates new skins and removes the burned ones. They answer the objection that an unoffending skin is punished by saying the skin does not feel; the person does, as “so they may taste the punishment” says. Here ghayr means different in an incompatible sense.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من أجرى الآية على ظاهرها

rows.speaker: أبو بكر
rows.claim: Abu Bakr says God clothes them in skins that transmit pain to their souls and hearts without themselves feeling it; he compares them to the tar garments in 14:50.
rows.anchor: واعتمد أبو بكر (¬4) هذا القول فقال: إن الله تعالى يلبسهم جلودا

rows.speaker: أبو النجم
rows.claim: Abu al-Najm's line about the prince replacing another prince illustrates exchanging one body for another, the sense of ibdāl.
rows.anchor: ومنه قول أبي النجم: عزل الأمير للأمير المبدل

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A more remote interpretation takes the skins as the tar garments of 14:50, called skins because they cling against the body.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من أبعد في التأويل فقال: أراد بالجلود السرابيل في قوله: {سرابيلهم من قطران}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression “skin” can name something closely associated with a person, as in a cited line about the skin between eye and nose.
rows.anchor: وجلدة بين العين والأنف سالم

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An anonymous poet calls garments “skins” in a line about Taim's green garments, supporting the adjacency interpretation.
rows.anchor: وينشد على هذا قول الشاعر: كسا اللؤم تيما خضرة في جلودها ... فويل لتيم من سرابيلها الخضر

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says a disbeliever's skin turns back into flesh and a new skin emerges from the flesh, so no skin that did not commit sin is substituted.
rows.anchor: وللسدي في هذا مذهب آخر، هو أنه قال: تبدل الجلود جلودا غيرها من لحم الكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naḍija means softened by heat, short of being burned through.
rows.anchor: ومعنى قوله: {كلما نضجت} أي لانت، والنضج هو اللين بالحرارة، وهو دون الاحتراق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naḍija is more forceful than “burned”: a fully burned skin cannot feel, and a pause between its destruction and renewal would relieve the unbeliever, whereas 2:162 says their punishment is not lightened or deferred.
rows.anchor: ولفظ النضج ههنا أبلغ في التعذيب من لفظ الإحراق؛ لأنها إذا احترقت لم تحس بألم
